title: Canetti as promoter; the percentage contract with Brunswick
summary: Canetti gave Briggs's group its first recording break on a percentage basis for Brunswick, which they suspected was shrewd, then promoted a concert at the Salle Pleyel.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well, then -- Canetti, I know, Canetti was writing for the Melody Maker, but he was basically a promoter, wasn't he?

Yes. He started to be a promoter. He started to be a promoter. He was a very intelligent person, very intelligent person, and he started booking bands, because he acted -- he didn't actually form the Harlemites, 'cause he gave us our first
*Lorenzo Tio was a famous pre-Armstrong New Orleans trumpeter trained formally and teacher of several of the city's musicians.
break, but we -- I don't know whether I should say this -- (Laughter).
I don't know whether I should have said --
Well, you can take it out later, if you want.

You see, he formed an orchestra. He didn't form the orchestra, but he gave us our first break to record. And, so far, he gave us a contract on a parietal basis (Laughter), and I imagine that's for recordings, but the only thing we were interested -- we were only interested in getting ourselves on wax.
Yeh, what was the basis -- how was the --
I don't know what that means.
Percentage. Oh, I see, you didn't get a flat fee?
Oh, I see. And this was for what company then?
I see, you mean, in other words, you didn't really trust Canetti, very much?
Yeh, 'cause in that contract -- I mean, on a percentage basis --
We found that out after, with the company.
You see. So, the only thing that interested us, we were recording, and we made some pretty good recordings.
Then he promoted a concert at the Salle de Pleyel, and it went over pretty nice.
